choices: A progressive neutrophil fall
Neutropenia warrants assessment, but the heparin-associated blood-count concern is the platelet trend.
A gradual hemoglobin rise
A rising hemoglobin does not indicate the platelet-related complication.
A rising eosinophil count
This is not the platelet fall associated with heparin-related complications.

procedure_timing.correct: Time and amount of the most recent dose
choices: Duration of the current anticoagulant course
The course duration provides context but does not establish the recent anticoagulant exposure before a procedure.
Time of the next planned routine dose
The next scheduled dose does not establish when the patient last received anticoagulation.
Total number of injections given this admission
The total number does not replace the timing and amount of the last dose.
Glass ampoule versus plastic vial packaging
Packaging does not establish the product strength or its suitability for therapeutic infusion.
Single-dose versus multidose container size
Container size does not distinguish therapeutic heparin from a flush formulation.
Brand-name versus generic-name label layout
The printed name does not replace verification of strength and intended product use.
Dose-related suppression of red-cell production
The sudden platelet fall specifically requires assessment for HIT.
Dilutional thrombocytopenia from a fluid load
Dilution can affect counts but must not explain away a new substantial fall during heparin therapy.
Platelet consumption attributed to the original illness
The illness is part of the differential, but heparin exposure requires consideration of HIT.

antithrombotic_combination.correct: Bleeding at visible and occult sites
choices: Progressive slowing of AV conduction
These treatments do not share AV-node blockade as their principal combined risk.
Rising potassium with falling urine output
Renal assessment matters, but it is not the shared antithrombotic effect being tested.
New muscle weakness with elevated creatine kinase
Muscle toxicity is not the shared effect of this antithrombotic combination.
Whether overlapping administration times explain peak effects
Timing can contribute, but the presence of two beta-blockers requires clarification of therapeutic duplication.
Whether the patient has missed recent antihypertensive doses
Missed doses may affect BP but do not explain the two active beta-blockers and slow pulse.
Whether the recorded pulse should be rechecked first
Rechecking supports assessment but does not resolve the duplicated prescribing issue.
duplicate_beta.stem: A patient already receiving a beta-blocker is prescribed {drug} and develops dizziness with a slow pulse. Which prescribing issue needs clarification?

choices: Additive vasodilation with compensatory tachycardia
Vasodilation does not explain the slow pulse and overlapping AV-node effects.
Increased preload with compensatory bradycardia
The relevant interaction is conduction slowing, not a primary increase in preload.
Reduced absorption of both cardiac medicines
Reduced exposure does not explain increased cardiac slowing.

tamsulosin_orthostasis.correct: Sitting and standing BP with symptoms
choices: A resting ECG with rhythm assessment
Rhythm assessment may be needed, but postural symptoms require checking BP with position.
Capillary glucose with symptom assessment
Glucose may be relevant to dizziness; the postural pattern specifically directs BP assessment.
Oxygen saturation with respiratory assessment
Oxygenation assessment does not directly test the suspected orthostatic effect.
tamsulosin_orthostasis.stem: A patient taking {drug} reports dizziness on standing. Which assessment most directly checks for an orthostatic adverse effect?

choices: Current or past antiplatelet exposure
Antiplatelet history is relevant to surgical planning, but the specific tamsulosin-related eye-surgery risk concerns its own exposure history.
Current or past inhaled steroid exposure
This does not identify the tamsulosin-related iris complication.
Current or past nitrate exposure
Nitrate use does not identify the tamsulosin-related iris complication.
tamsulosin_ifis.stem: A patient is scheduled for cataract surgery. Which medication history specifically alerts the team to the iris complication associated with {drug}?

tamsulosin_distal_stone.correct: Helping passage of distal ureteral stones
choices: Dissolving uric-acid stones by alkalinizing urine
Tamsulosin does not work by urinary alkalinization or chemical stone dissolution.
Reducing urine production during acute renal colic
Its selected stone use is not based on suppressing urine production.
Eradicating urinary infection around an obstructing stone
Tamsulosin is not an antibacterial treatment for infected obstruction.

alteplase_screen.correct: Brain imaging excluding hemorrhage with protocol eligibility review
choices: A neurological score establishing the severity of deficits
Severity assessment is needed, but it does not exclude intracranial hemorrhage or establish complete eligibility.
A symptom-onset time within the treatment window
Timing is needed, but does not replace brain imaging and the full eligibility assessment.
A blood-pressure reading within the protocol limits
BP is part of screening; an acceptable reading does not exclude hemorrhage or satisfy all eligibility criteria.

alteplase_followup.correct: The authorized post-thrombolysis assessment and follow-up imaging plan
choices: A normal platelet count with no visible bleeding
These findings do not replace the authorized post-thrombolysis assessment and imaging requirements.
Improvement in the initial neurological deficit
Clinical improvement does not independently clear the patient for antithrombotic therapy.
Completion of the prescribed alteplase infusion
Infusion completion is not sufficient clearance for antithrombotic treatment.

insulin_route.correct: Correction is generally SC; IV insulin follows a separate controlled protocol
choices: Correction and IV insulin share the same units-to-volume calculation
Concentration and delivery differ; one calculation cannot establish equivalence of the protocols.
Correction and IV insulin use the same bedside-glucose dosing table
An SC correction scale must not be assumed to define an IV infusion protocol.
Correction is generally IV; the SC route is reserved for basal insulin
Ordinary correction insulin is generally SC, while IV treatment follows a separate protocol.

insulin_meals.correct: Current glucose, insulin product, prescribed scale, and NPO status
choices: Usual home insulin dose and the time of the previous meal
Home dosing and prior meals do not establish the current prescribed correction decision.
Most recent HbA1c and the planned daily calorie intake
Longer-term information does not replace current glucose, order, product and NPO assessment.
Yesterday’s glucose trend and the usual inpatient meal schedule
Yesterday’s pattern does not establish the patient’s current glucose or canceled-meal status.

glucose_recheck.correct: Repeat glucose with consciousness and symptoms
choices: Repeat BP with peripheral perfusion
Circulation needs reassessment, but BP cannot establish whether the glucose abnormality has corrected.
Repeat respiratory rate with oxygen saturation
Breathing assessment does not establish the glucose response.
Repeat neurological assessment without glucose measurement
Symptoms may improve but do not replace an objective glucose recheck.
Reduced nitrate absorption with loss of antianginal effect
The key interaction concern is enhanced hypotension, not reduced absorption.
Additive platelet inhibition with gastrointestinal bleeding
The key interaction is not combined antiplatelet activity.
Additive AV-node blockade with severe bradycardia
These medicines are not combined primarily through AV-node blockade.

sl_tablet.correct: Let it dissolve under the tongue
choices: Swallow it whole with a glass of water
Swallowing does not follow the intended sublingual route.
Keep it between the cheek and gum until dissolved
Buccal placement is a different administration site from the prescribed sublingual route.
Chew it thoroughly before swallowing
Chewing and swallowing do not follow the documented sublingual administration.
An additional magnesium dose
Additional magnesium can worsen the suspected toxicity.
A potassium replacement dose
Potassium is not the emergency antagonist for significant magnesium effects.
A sodium bicarbonate dose
Bicarbonate is not the specific antagonist being tested.
magnesium_calcium.stem: Which treatment may be ordered to counter the neuromuscular and respiratory depression caused by excessive IV magnesium?

choices: Open-angle glaucoma with a stable bowel pattern
The particular antimuscarinic concern is narrow-angle glaucoma and urinary retention.
Controlled reflux with a history of iron deficiency
These are not the specific antimuscarinic cautions being tested.
Recurrent renal colic with normal bladder emptying
This does not identify the urinary-retention or narrow-angle glaucoma caution.
